title: Phase-dependent kink collisions and dual critical-velocity branches in the complex sine-Gordon model
authors: Mohammad Mohammadi, Farnaz Eizadbaksh, Vahideh Bagheri
abstract: The complex sine-Gordon (CSG) model contains an internal phase degree of freedom that strongly modifies the dynamics of its solitary-wave solutions. We present a numerical study of complex kink--kink collisions and determine how the final state depends jointly on the initial velocity and relative phase. In contrast with the elastic collisions of the real sine-Gordon model, the CSG system exhibits scattering, capture, long-lived bion formation, breather-like states, and emission of radiative profiles. The simulations reveal two distinct phase-dependent branches of critical velocity. In one branch, increasing the initial velocity promotes capture, whereas in the other it restores scattering. This dual structure highlights the rich velocity--phase dependence of the collision dynamics. We also compute the energy carried by radiative profiles and examine extreme values of the energy density, kinetic and gradient contributions, and field modulus at the collision center. These quantities show sharp transitions at critical points and provide sensitive diagnostics of phase-controlled dynamics. These results suggest that the relative phase behaves as an effective internal degree of freedom that plays an important role in the collision dynamics of complex solitons.
summary: This work numerically analyzes kink collisions in the Complex Sine-Gordon model, showing that the system's dynamics are highly sensitive to the relative phase between colliding kinks. Unlike simpler models, the CSG exhibits a dual critical velocity structure where increasing initial speed can lead either to capture or scattering depending on the phase. This highlights the crucial role of internal symmetries in determining soliton interaction outcomes.
main_problem: The study investigates complex kink-kink collisions within the Complex Sine-Gordon (CSG) model to determine how the final state depends on both initial relative velocity and phase.
main_result: The CSG system exhibits rich dynamics, including scattering, capture, and bion formation, characterized by two distinct phase-dependent branches of critical velocity that contrast sharply with real sine-Gordon models.
method: Numerical simulations are employed to model the time evolution of the complex scalar field during collisions, analyzing energy density components and radiative emission.
model_or_system: The system is governed by the Complex Sine-Gordon (CSG) model, which generalizes the real SG theory using a complex scalar field $\phi$. This introduces an internal phase degree of freedom ($	heta$) that dictates collision outcomes.
key_observables: Collision outcomes (scattering vs. capture), energy carried by radiative profiles, and extreme values of energy density components ($k_{max}, u_{max}, R_{max}$) at the collision center.
important_parameters: Initial relative phase ($\Delta	heta$) and initial velocity ($v$), which define two distinct critical velocity branches (red/blue).
main_assumptions: The use of linear superposition as an approximation for initial kink conditions, and numerical limitations restricting measurements to certain time scales.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of collision outcomes on phase and velocity, showing regimes of capture versus scattering, and visualizing energy density profiles and radiative emission over time.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the CSG model's complexity due to its internal phase, detailing numerical methods for simulating collisions, presenting diagnostics like radiation energy ratios, and finally mapping out the dual critical velocity structure based on initial conditions.
why_interesting: The concept of an 'effective internal degree of freedom' (the phase) controlling macroscopic dynamics like soliton collision outcomes is relevant to understanding complex order parameters in condensed matter systems or quantum field theories with internal symmetries.
